subtopic: TRANSFER FROM UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE COMMISSION TO DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: TRANSFER FROM UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE COMMISSION TO DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I should like to inform the house that arrangements have now been completed for the transfer of the national employment service from the unemployment insurance commission to the Department of Labour as of April 1.
The decision to effect this transfer was taken by the government following a recommendation of the Gill committee which inquired into the operations carried on under the Unemployment Insurance Act. The broad lines of the division of the existing staff of the unemployment insurance commission have been determined partly on the basis of those positions which were concerned mainly or exclusively with insurance matters on the one hand and with employment matters on the other, and partly on a fair and reasonable distribution of the remaining positions which are concerned with joint services affecting both insurance and unemployment activities.
On the basis of this distribution some 4,156 positions are being transferred as of April 1 to the Department of Labour, and 5,859 positions will remain with the unemployment insurance commission. Assurance has been given to all those who are remaining in the unemployment insurance commission as well as those joining the Department of Labour that the transfer will not adversely affect them. It has been agreed with the civil service commission that competitions for positions in either the unemployment insurance commission or in the Department of Labour will be open to the personnel of both during the next live years.
20220-822J
It will be appreciated that the transfer has been by no means an easy one to bring about, and I want to express my appreciation for the co-operation of all concerned.
In addition to reaching decisions about a reasonable distribution of staff, decisions have had to be made with respect to a fair allocation of equipment and other facilities and space. It will not be possible nor practical to implement all these decisions with respect to office accommodation and equipment on April 1. It will take some time before all of them can be implemented, but in the meantime the basic objectives have been determined.
Another important matter that has been examined carefully is the continuing close liaison needed between the operations of the national employment service and the unemployment insurance commission. A number of transitional steps have been taken to assist in the transfer and to ensure continuity of service to the public in both employment service and insurance operations. The director of the national employment service in the unemployment insurance commission will become the national director of the national employment service in the Department of Labour. The regional offices of the national employment service, each one of which will have its own regional director, will report directly to the national director.
Additional positions will be required to strengthen the staff of the national employment service at head office and, where they are immediately needed, elsewhere. We expect to be in a position to place our requirements before the treasury board in the very near future. The classification of employment officer positions is also under active review with the civil service commission.
We intend to have a thorough study made, with the help of independent advisers, of the reorganization of the national employment service to ensure that it will become the key operational agency in the manpower field. This independent and objective analysis will also include an assessment of the other manpower activities in the Department of Labour, and of the most effective ways and means of achieving a fully co-ordinated, over-all manpower program in Canada. These steps will be taken immediately.

National Employment Service
I have stressed the need for an aggressive and positive manpower policy ever since I became Minister of Labour. I have also welcomed the strong emphasis which the economic council of Canada has placed on manpower as a major part of economic policy, and I fully agree with the stress they have placed on the need for close co-ordination of all programs and policies in this field.
We have made significant progress in developing an over-all Canadian manpower policy, and have already achieved a substantial amount of co-ordination. The transfer of the national employment service to the Department of Labour on April 1 will mean that most essential elements of manpower policy at the federal level will be under the Minister of Labour.
This transfer and the other steps I have announced today will make a further contribution toward realization of an active and fully co-ordinated manpower policy, a major element in our country's total economic and social development.

subtopic: TRANSFER FROM UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE COMMISSION TO DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks on the announcement just made by the Minister of Labour will be brief.
One of the recommendations the Gill commission made to the government was that the national employment service of the unemployment insurance commission be transferred to the Department of Labour. When considering the minister's announcement in respect of this recommendation we must at the same time wonder why the government has not taken action on the other recommendations which the Gill commission made to the government. The one the subject of this announcement is only one of a great many that should be considered. As a matter of fact the government have not even told the house or the people of the country what they intend to do about the balance of these recommendations, and it is very important to the people of the country that the government make an announcement soon as to their intentions with respect to them.
I think the government should advise us as to what role the national employment service will play in the Department of Labour. As the minister has pointed out, this will be a very important part of the work of the Department of Labour so far as manpower policy is concerned. In view of this fact, what position will the head of the national employment service hold in the administrative set-up of the Department of Labour? I think he should be at least an assistant deputy minister in the department
[Mr. MacEachen.)
so this division of the department will have some prestige and will be recognized as a very essential and potent aspect of the department.
With regard to the matter of liaison between the unemployment insurance commission and the national employment service, I think that should be carried out because the two have a great deal to do with one another, however, the national employment service should be foremost rather than the unemployment insurance commission. This is something I stressed when I was minister of labour, and at that time I think we were coming out of the shell and giving more emphasis to the employment service rather than to the unemployment insurance commission.
The minister always brings up in the house the work that has been done, particularly in the Department of Labour, with regard to the manpower policy of the government. Yet nothing has been clearly stated as to the achievements. Even today the Minister of Labour said there has been co-ordination across the country as a result of the establishment of the manpower committee, but he leaves us in the dark as to the results of this co-ordination. I hope that in the very near future the Minister of Labour will be more frank with us and tell us specifically what co-ordination has been brought about with respect to manpower policy by the manpower committee that has been set up in his department.

subtopic: TRANSFER FROM UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE COMMISSION TO DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose the first thing one might say about the minister's statement is that it is much better than we expected on the basis of similar statements he has been making in reply to questions in recent months. The economic council has been very critical of the government's manpower policies, in that to meet the requirements of our rapidly changing economy the employment service must have the means to promote the mobility of Canada's labour force. In its recent presentation to the government the Canadian Labour Congress suggested that the national employment service should really become Canada's national manpower service. It also suggested that if the manpower service is going to do the job it has to have the ability to collect labour market information on a nation-wide and continuous basis, accompanied by professional analysis and detailed forecasting of labour market trends.

Despite this kind of thinking and proposals of this nature, the minister has continued until today to suggest that while he intended to announce that the national employment service would come under the jurisdiction of his department, the Department of Labour would continue as it has up to now and that the manpower consultative service would continue as in the past. The result would be to continue the kind of fragmented set-up we have had and which every other agency, except the minister and his department, had predicted would lead to disaster.
So it was good to hear the minister say the department is going to have a very careful look at the co-ordination and co-operation of these various services. I wish the minister could have had this done before he made his announcement today, and I think he could have if he had acted much more forthrightly.
There is one more thing that in my opinion needs to be kept in mind. If the national employment service is going to do the job we expect it to do, it will have to have the kind of staff it has not had up to now.
I saw an announcement recently that they had provision for only one economist in their complement, and that position is vacant at the present time. Certainly if they are going to do the job which is required they are going to have to have the technical and professional staff which will give them the information required in order to direct people to jobs and find jobs for people. I hope the minister's statement today will be followed by some real action in the next few months.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the long statement of the Minister of Labour, which we did not have the opportunity to consider beforehand, of course, I should like to make a few brief comments, rather critical but objective, however, in this connection.
It seems that this decision stems from the Gill and Glassco reports. Both reports had recommended changes in the administration of the Department of Labour and in the field of unemployment insurance and employment.
It is certainly an excellent decision made by the minister to separate definitely the employment section from the unemployment insurance, as such, and to integrate it into the Department of Labour.
What concrete results can we expect? Naturally, that is a bit difficult to determine at this time.
National Employment Service
Considering the recommendations in the report submitted by the economic council of Canada before Christmas, and faced with the possible recession forecast for next year, I think it is a good thing that the government take steps to train the workers for the new jobs that could be made available to them.
However, there is one point especially to which I should like to draw the minister's attention, as regards this particular training program for workers. The program was controlled by the unemployment insurance commission, which was responsible for paying certain allowances to workers so they might register at technical schools and be trained to take other jobs in other economic fields.
The minister will be able to entrust that new branch of his department which will look after employment with the specific task of setting up an adequate program which would be flexible enough to apply to all areas.
For my part, I have received representations from the authorities of my region to the effect that the formula tried out last year for the retraining of workers did not meet the requirements of our area.
I appreciate the difficulty of finding a formula applicable everywhere. However, I feel that is the objective the minister and his department should strive to reach because that is one of the best solutions to the problem of retraining workers. In this era of automation we must all anticipate that workers will have to be retrained in order to be able to take jobs in other fields of endeavour or other trades.
There is also another aspect which should be changed, and that is the formula under which the number of unemployed is arrived at. Every month the minister informs the house of the number of unemployed according to the figures published by the bureau of statistics. I have always wondered why he did not use the reports submitted to him by all local unemployment insurance offices to determine the actual number of unemployed. Instead, a sampling formula is used which I think does not reflect the facts as they are. I think the minister should have more confidence in the monthly reports submitted to him by the managers of some 260 unemployment insurance offices throughout Canada.
That is all I wanted to say and I hope that the minister will consider the possibility of using those reports to establish exactly the number of unemployed in the various areas of the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attentiveness to the declaration of the Minister of Labour and, as the hon. member for Lake St. John said, it is a pretty long statement that covers a lot of territory.
I would have liked to see it in written form so that hon. members could give better consideration to it by way of criticism or approval. As the minister stated, and as was reiterated by the hon. member for Ontario, this declaration is based on one of the recommendations in the Gill report. Many questions have been asked of the minister about an opportunity to study the Gill report thoroughly. As I say, this deals with one of the recommendations in that report, but what about the rest of the recommendations? When will they be put into effect? There may be some good in this, in fact there must be, but we have to watch the catches in each corner.
Yesterday I asked the minister a question about this business of closing down small offices and transferring their functions to central offices. Where a number of these employment offices have been closed down across the country it has caused greater expense to the unemployed. Their closing might provide better organization for the bureaucratic system we have, but there will be less benefits at the bottom, at least to a certain extent.
I am wondering if this is not just a hitch between the federal government and the provincial governments, because the latter are opening unemployment offices. With the transfer of manpower and labour force responsibilities to the Department of Labour, leaving unemployment to be dealt with by a separate office, I ask what co-ordination is there between the provinces and the federal Department of Labour? Is this giving them permission to provide a little more local patronage? That is why I want to see to the bottom of this thing.
I know that in the province of Quebec a lot of these little establishments are popping up. As the federal government closes down its offices, provincial establishments are popping up and I would like to get some explanation for that. I shall not stress the matter at the moment as I shall have more time to deal with it during discussion of the supply motion, and possibly some explanations can be given when we enter the throne speech debate. In the meantime this is still a question into which we must look.
[Mr. Lessard (Lake St. John) .1
On the other hand, if by this transfer of manpower to the Department of Labour, and if through some of the programs which have been put into effect during the past year or two the country or the unemployed are helped, then I would ask the minister to guard against one thing, namely not to be too bureaucratic about it but rather to be a little bit practical and humanitarian. At present there is a tendency to switch the unemployed and their families from one end of the country to another, like cattle going to the stock market. It might be a good thing to re-establish an unemployed person in an area where he can get work, but we should not be inhuman about it. I know the minister will himself be human, but there are some bureaucrats who cannot be called that. The policy involved will have to be clear, with recommendations and regulations carefully laid down so that bureaucrats will not get strange ideas, wishing to make extra work for themselves, and thus put their feet in a trap. I would ask the minister to ensure that the law with respect to this declaration is made clear, so this new policy will not in effect mean one door in and four doors out, and so that when it goes into effect it will benefit the people concerned.

1. Oceanographic, hydrographic, submarine geological and geophysical investigations are being planned for this summer in Hudson bay on a joint project involving marine sciences branch; geological survey branch; observatories branch.

speechtext: Has the marine post office at Port Colbome been closed, and, if so, what alternative arrangements, if any, are being made for postal services for Canadian sailors on the great lakes?

subtopic: MARINE POST OFFICE, PORT COLBORNE, ONT.
speechtext: Yes. The decision to close the Port Colborne marine post office was taken in close cooperation with the St. Lawrence seaway authority. With the renovation of the Welland canal system, and with the aim of the authority to speed up traffic, ships will no longer be permitted to stop to transact business within the canal nor will crew members be permitted to go ashore. With these points in mind, it will no longer be practicable to operate a post office on the canal system. In future, mail for those concerned should be addressed to the ports of call or in care of the shipping company.

Perhaps, I could go through the resolutions briefly and give some explanation. It will be noted that an additional eight twelfths of the external affairs vote, item 15 of the main estimates is being requested. This item has to do with Canada's contribution to a series of international funds, and as these payments are made at the start of the fiscal year, the amounts are needed now.
Then, the next item is an additional five twelfths of external affairs item 20 of the main estimates. This provides for contributions to the programs of the NATO science committee, the international civil aviation organization, grants to the international Red Cross, the commonwealth institute and the UN training and research institute. An additional portion is required to relieve the financial position of certain international agencies.
The next additional amount requested is four twelfths of the total amount of Atomic Energy item 5 of the main estimates. This is the vote in those estimates for providing assistance to universities. The arrangements with the universities call for paying half the amount early in the fiscal year.
Then, the next additional amount being requested is three twelfths of national research council item 10 of the main estimates. This vote provides for payment of scholarships and grants in aid of research to

Canadian universities. A large part of these grants is made early in the fiscal year.
The next additional amount being requested is under Legislation item 20 and has to do with the cost of operating the House of Commons. Since the costs are higher when the house is not in recess, and it is expected it will be sitting in May and June, the request is made for that reason.
Then, there is Mines and Technical Surveys item 25; Secretary of State item 30 and Transport item 95 of the main estimates. The Mines and Technical Surveys item has to do with field surveys. The one for the Secretary of State department has to do with paying for a carryover of the cost of the memorial centre in Charlottetown, an overdue bill. Then, the Transport item is connected with the Canadian maritime commission and deals with ship subsidies. There are a number of ships at the point where substantial payments have to be made in the first two months of the year to meet the construction program. These payments come at irregular intervals and it so happens an abnormally high proportion of them are due in the next two months.
Then, the last additional item requested is for an additional one twelfth of the total amounts of External Affairs item 5; Justice item 1; Legislation item 5; Mines and Technical Surveys items 10, 15, 45, 50 and 60; National Revenue item 5 and Trade and Commerce item 15 of the main estimates. The item concerning External Affairs has to do with supplying certain posts abroad. The item in Justice has to do with the federal government's requirement for providing for the costs of territorial governments which are later recovered from them. The item having to do with Legislation has to do with sessional requirements of the Senate. Then, the Mines and Technical Surveys items have to do with surveying activities. These surveying activities are undertaken early in the summer and costs are incurred during the better weather. There will be more than two twelfths required in the first two months of the new fiscal year. The National Revenue items have to do with the unpleasant fact that we have to pay our income taxes in April and there is the added cost for hiring of additional staff. The Trade and Commerce item has to do with the spring and summer advertising campaign of the travel bureau. This is undertaken at the start of the tourist season each year.
I believe that, with these explanations, I have covered the reasons for making the requests we are making. I do not know that

there is much more I can usefully add at this stage, except to state that the bill based on this resolution is in the usual form for the interim supply bill. Of course, I will give the formal undertaking that the adoption of the resolution will not abridge the rights and privileges of members to criticize any item in the estimates when they come up for consideration in committee of supply. The rights and privileges of members will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as the result of the passing of this measure.
I was just going to ask for that undertaking, the usual formal undertaking. The President of the Privy Council having given it, there is no other comment I have to make at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the opportunity, under interim supply, of bringing to the attention of this committee and the people of Canada a very important economic situation with which we are confronted in the agreement relating to concessions on automotive products between Canada and the government of the United States of America. This is the first opportunity this house has had of bringing the matter to the attention of the government. The agreement is a masterpiece of complexity. It has brought about considerable excitement and a great amount of interest in the country. It has been referred to as a piece of bold negotiation, and I believe that is right. I am also of the opinion the agreement was reached without realizing many of the pitfalls which are now being revealed.
Mr. Chairman, there is a lot at stake. We are certainly tinkering with the manufacture of a very important product in this country. It is important because all Canadians have a stake in the impact of this treaty on car prices, and the employment picture. It will affect many people who have a close, personal involvement in it. It will have far reaching effects on related industries in our country. The matter of freer trade is an aspect of this agreement, as is the matter of trade balance. I say, therefore, it is of great importance to the country as a whole. It is important because seven departments of the government were involved in drafting this treaty with the United States.
The Department of Industry, the Department of Finance, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Labour, the Department of External Affairs, the Department of National Revenue and the De-

partment of Justice were all involved in drafting this treaty, yet the responsibility for it falls on the shoulders of one person, the Minister of Industry. He is the man who must accept the blame, or the man who will accept any credit that might come from it. He backed it, and for all I know he may have backed into it.
We have not got all the picture, but on the surface it would appear to be a complete sell-out to the United States so far as the automotive and car parts industry is concerned. All the negotiations took place in the United States. It was a matter of David and Goliath, and it remains to be seen who will come out of it as David and who as Goliath. It is important to all parts of Canada, but of particular interest to the province of Ontario because 97 per cent of the automotive and car parts industry is located in that province.
I ask, why was this brought about by a treaty? Why by order in council? Why was parliament circumvented? Why were we, the elected representatives of the people, ignored? Why had we no opportunity to debate this important subject, one that has such far reaching economic consequences?
When I return to my riding and somebody asks me "What about this car parts and car manufacturing agreement with the United States?" I must admit I do not know much about it, because we did not have a chance to debate it in the House of Commons. That is the way the government chose to do it, and I am at a loss to know why they did not bring this treaty before parliament for full scale debate before signing it.
It is a matter of an independent nation such as Canada going down to the United States and having a conference with the three big car manufacturers. It was a matter of their getting together and talking it over, and then going to President Johnson and saying, "Sign this, because it is good for the United States. It is good for the industry. Go ahead and sign it." This would seem to be the way it was done. The Canadian representatives even went down to President Johnson's farm. There they had a good time and signed the treaty, while we, the elected representatives, remained at home and were told nothing about this very important treaty.
What has it to do with the commonwealth preference? Following the signing of this treaty, U.K. cars which had the privilege of coming into Canada duty free were faced with immediate competition from cars imported duty free from the United States. This
Interim Supply
brings up the problem of GATT. Member nations of GATT say this is not within keeping of the terms of GATT, and they expect to be accorded similar free treatment, as is their right as members of GATT. Under the terms of GATT, any member nation which gives special privileges to any other member must give the same opportunity to all members. So far as I can see it is a one-way street. It took effect in Canada right away on January 18, but it will not take effect in the United States until congress meets and discusses it. That is why I say it is a oneway street.
I would now like to refer to the constitutional picture, and ask the government why it did not give us the opportunity to debate the treaty in this house? That has not been the policy of Liberal governments in the past. On the constitutional question, the proper procedure to be followed in cases such as this is indicated under the British and Canadian constitutions. The crown enjoys the sole right of conduct on foreign relations which includes the making and, if necessary, ratification of international agreements of all kinds.
It is a rare thing in the United Kingdom for the government to ask the approval of parliament, in the house of commons, before making or ratifying treaties, even formal and important ones; but we in Canada have not followed this principle. Without derogating from the legal rights of the crown, a custom has developed in Canada different from that in the United Kingdom.
On June 21, 1926 the Canadian House of Commons adopted a resolution moved by the then prime minister, Mackenzie King, the final paragraph of which read, that the house considers that-
-before His Majesty's Canadian ministers advise ratification of a treaty or convention affecting Canada, or signify acceptance of any treaty, convention or agreement involving military or economic sanctions, the approval of the parliament of Canada should be secured.
On April 12, 1928, in the course of the debate on the international sanitary convention, the same right hon. gentleman had this to say:
I submit that the day has passed when any government or executive should feel that they should take it upon themselves without the approval of parliament, to commit a country to obligations involving any considerable financial outlays or active undertakings. In all cases where obligations of such a character are being assumed internationally, parliament itself should be assured of having the full right of approving what is done before binding commitments are made. I would not confine parliamentary approval only to those matters which involve military sanctions and the

Interim Supply
like. I feel parliamentary approval should apply where there are Involved matters of large expenditure or political considerations of a far reaching character.
That was the attitude of a Liberal government in former days, seeking more parliamentary control over international agreements.
On April 9,	1962, the present Prime
Minister when he was leader of the opposition had this to say in debating the Columbia river agreement:
Well, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that this treaty, before ratification, should go before the committee on external affairs.
Then he went on to say:
I tell the prime minister-
Referring to the present right hon. Leader of the Opposition.
-that the committee on external affairs considered every important treaty while we were in office.
Now what do we find? This government, with a new group of nine cabinet members who were formerly senior civil servants, does not think in terms like that. It goes ahead and negotiates treaties without giving us the right to discuss them in parliament.
I should now like to review briefly the matter of removing duty on agricultural implements, as introduced by the Liberal government in 1944, and may I say I think that in order to substantiate debate and consideration of new ideas one should always refer to the pages of history to see if he is on firm ground. At that time the Liberal member for Brantford city, who is presently a senator, had this to say when talking about removing the duty on agricultural implements imported into Canada, and this is to be found on page 5155 of Hansard for July 20, 1944:
I referred to the removal of the duty on agricultural implements when the budget was being debated in the house. At that time I said that X could not approve it. I have given the matter careful consideration since, and I am still opposed to the removal of the duty on agricultural implements.
Then he went on to say:
-the removal of the duty might have a detrimental effect on the workers in these factories.
He felt at that time that, contrary to what was the general belief, if the tariff was removed Canada would reap a greater share of the manufacturing of agricultural implements in this country. This seems to be the belief in the car industry as well. But I would remind the minister that this was not the case in the agricultural implements business. Canada got the short end of the stick. We did not get nearly the share of the manu-

facturing of agricultural implements that we were supposed to get or that people thought we would get. As a matter of fact, from the year 1944, when the duty of 7J per cent was removed, the production of agricultural implements in the United States increased about six times, and production in Canada only increased a little over four times. So in that case the United States had the opportunity, and took advantage of it, of manufacturing more agricultural implements and shipping them into Canada duty free. The same thing can happen in the car industry.
I would like to say at the outset, Mr. Chairman, that this party has always been the party that took into consideration the automotive industry and had full respect and thought for that industry. Who was it that removed the sales tax on automobiles? We were the party that removed it. I know that the Liberals reduced it, and I also know that when they reduced it they were the party that left the car dealer with stock on hand holding the bag for the sales tax they had paid. When we reduced the sales tax and then removed it completely, we compensated the car dealer for any stock that he had on hand. If anybody wishes to confer with any car dealer or car manufacturer in this country, I think he will be told that this party gave them a very, very square deal on the removing of the sales tax.
To understand fully this treaty one must go back some years to the introduction of the Bladen report. Again I say, Mr. Chairman, that it was a Conservative government which set up this one-man commission. Professor Bladen brought down a report so simple in its explanation and outline that it is a wonder it had not been done years before. At that time no automatic transmissions were being made in Canada, and the Conservative government decided to allow the automotive companies to bring automatic transmissions into this country and to remit the duty on them to the extent that the value of the imports was counterbalanced by exports of Canadian-made automotive parts to the United States. This move was designed to increase the manufacture of car parts in Canada, and worked extremely well.
When the Liberal government took office the Drury mark I plan was introduced. Under this plan the privilege of claiming rebate of duty on imports from the United States was extended to all car parts, once again to the extent that the imports were counterbalanced by exports of Canadian-made parts. A clause was also inserted which required that to

qualify for such a privilege the car manufacturer must maintain a commonwealth, essentially Canadian, content of at least 60 per cent in the vehicles he sold in Canada. Naturally, the plan was somewhat more complicated than this, but these were the essentials of the mark 1 Drury plan. The effect of this plan hurt some parts companies in the United States. That is understandable. One particular company, the Modine Radiator Company, decided to take legal action. The company held that the plan amounted to dumping and applied to congress for the imposition of countervailing duties, which would have the same effect as the reimposition of the customs tariff. Naturally, had congress granted this request the mark I Drury plan would have been dead.
In anticipation of the decision of congress- the case has been heard but the decision has not been announced as yet, to my knowledge -negotiations were started between the Canadian and the United States governments for a plan which would replace the one about to collapse. I do not know who commenced the negotiations but I would strongly suspect that it was the American people who instituted them. During these discussions the automotive parts manufacturers association was consulted somewhat reluctantly by the government, but little heed was paid to their recommendations favourable to Canadian owned industries. It should also be remembered that many of the members of the automotive parts manufacturers association are United States controlled and, to say the least, would have divided loyalties.
Under the new Drury mark II plan the privilege was given to automobile manufacturers, and to them only, to import cars and parts for original equipment manufacture free of duty into Canada, provided they fulfilled certain conditions. Again I say this treaty is wrapped up in complexity, Mr. Chairman, I think you will agree to this when I bring the following to the attention of hon. members. These conditions were: First, that they made vehicles of the type now being considered in the base year, August 1, 1962 to July 31, 1964; second, that they maintained at least the same proportion of cars made in Canada to cars sold in Canada as pertained in the base year, and in any case not less than 75 per cent; and third, that they maintained at least the same Canadian content as they had in the base year. It is in this third condition that there lies the source of trouble.
Under the mark I plan the Canadian content had to be at least 60 per cent, and say a company sold cars to the value of $100 million,
Interim Supply
the Canadian content in parts, labour and overhead had to be at least $60 million. Under the new mark II plan, the same company can increase the number of cars manufactured to a value of, say $200 million, and still maintain only a Canadian content of $60 million. If I do not understand this properly, Mr. Chairman, I would like the minister to correct me. However, I asked him questions in the house earlier about changing the dollar value to a percentage value and he accepted my questions as though they were in order. I will say to the minister that I am in some doubt in this respect, namely as to whether with regard to this increase of $100 million, 60 per cent of the increase has to be composed of Canadian content. It is logical that the manufacturer should purchase all the parts he requires from his own subsidiary in the United States, where the volume of production is at least ten times greater than that pertaining in Canada, with the result that prices are greatly reduced. This is only common sense and good business. He can then import these parts duty free into Canada, build them into cars and sell those cars either in Canada or the United States. He does two things. First, he increases his operation in his parts producing plant in the United States, thus increasing his profits because increased production means that unit cost goes down. In the second place, he increases his assembly operations in Canada so as to maintain his Canadian content. Once again, he has increased his profit.
I know the minister will tell us that this plan will create lots of jobs-9,000 jobs I think he said. Well, it may create some jobs on the assembly lines, which call chiefly for unskilled workers. If this is the kind of employment the government wants, with its ups and downs, its seasonal fluctuations, it is possible they will get it, but I do not think this policy is good logic. As against this increase which the minister expects in the assembly side of the business-and I for one am doubtful about it-what about the Canadian owned auto parts manufacturers who will have to lay off hundreds of people? What about the purchasing departments of the three main companies in Canada-perhaps I should confine their number to two which are considered as something more than United States subsidiaries? What necessity will they have for retaining their purchasing departments in Canada? They will no longer be necessary. They can close them down and do all their business from head offices in the United States, as a consequence of which

Interim Supply
people here will be laid off work. When these considerations are balanced out I doubt whether there will be any increase in employment such as the minister has suggested.
Since all these various profits have now been diverted to United States owned companies-and this is a fact-the result can only be rapidly increased domination of Canadian industry by United States capital and the disappearance of Canadian owned companies. I am surprised that the Minister of Industry should have adopted a policy which would go so far as to allow the takeover of Canadian owned companies by United States operators, particularly when his colleague the Minister of Finance has gone out of his way to do everything humanly possible to maintain Canadian ownership of the factories in this country.
This is another example of legislation at cross purposes. Indeed, I have never seen a government which has engaged in so much legislation at cross purposes as has this one. For example, the Minister of Agriculture made a subsidy on tobacco available, and at the same time the Minister of National Health and Welfare spends $700,000 to tell people not to smoke the weed. The Minister of Labour said he wanted firms to employ men aged 45 and over, and the government spent $3 million odd to encourage the employment of men in this age group. This resulted in the employment of only 2,000 people; it was in force for five months at a cost to the taxpayer of more than $3 million. The Minister of Justice was asked in this house whether his department employed men aged 45 years and over, and he replied: "No, that is not our policy". There are other examples of this cross purpose legislation, but they escape my mind at the moment. The subject I have been discussing is a typical example. One minister says we must encourage our Canadian owned industries while another says: "Come on in, boys, the coast is clear. Start up your manufacturing, the gates are open."
The Minister of Industry tells us that the three automotive corporations, General Motors, Ford and Chrysler have undertaken in writing to increase their Canadian content above that which was achieved in the base year. However, these undertakings, if they exist, are in the form of confidential letters from the presidents of the car companies; they are secret and, since they are no part of the plan, they are not enforceable. We do not have access to these letters. I have two motions on the order paper asking for them-
The press do.

One of my hon. friends says the press has access to their letters. If members of the press are entitled to see them, surely we as members of parliament should be entitled to see them. But I am advised that it is very doubtful whether we will have the opportunity to see these documents affecting this important industry.
There are two other aspects of the situation which must be considered deplorable. It is deplorable that the Canadian government should have negotiated an agreement of such far reaching scope and rely for its results on private arrangements with the presidents of three foreign corporations. Second, it must be considered deplorable that at no time has this plan been discussed by the elected members of parliament. The government decided to treat this matter as involving merely a reduction in tariffs and was thus able to introduce these arrangements by order in council.
There is much more that could be said on this subject, a subject of great complexity and far reaching consequences. I know there are other hon. members who wish to speak on it. I simply ask these questions: Why did we not have an opportunity to discuss a matter of this importance? Why was this brought about by order in council when members of this government themselves suggested that far reaching arrangements such as this should be made by treaty and discussed in the house? In my humble opinion this agreement has brought about free trade for the producer but not free trade for the consumer.
A free ride.

It may be a free ride for some, too, as one of my hon. friends has said. This represents a $50 million loss to Canada on the basis of last year's imports worth $600 million, subject to a duty of 17J per cent on cars and 25 per cent on parts. This money has been put into the pockets of the car producers. Canadians pay the same for their new cars-there is no mistake about that- and the Canadian manufacturer keeps the change.
Shame.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What does the Liberal party get out of this?

There are an awful lot of answers still to come and I am sure other hon. members are anxious to speak on this subject. I understand this agreement is coming before the U.S. congress shortly. What

will happen if congress does not approve of this arrangement? Will our tariffs be put back as they were, or will a free tariff situation continue? There are a hundred and one questions members could ask, and we have a right to know the answers. But there has been no chance to debate this subject, no opportunity for the elected representatives of the people to express their views.

My colleagues have asked me to express on behalf of this group the attitude we are adopting at this time, and perhaps I may do so by making what one might call a non-speech. We have the hope-and it is shared by others in the house-that we can complete interim supply quickly and that hon. members who feel they must call attention to certain subjects and raise certain points should raise them on the supplementary estimates, to the end that we might almost guarantee clearing up the work of this session as soon as possible.
I realize this is sometimes a large order. I can certainly understand why the previous speaker felt obliged to make the case he did. I appreciate, too, that he made the case very well. But in these circumstances there is, one might say, a Pandora's box which could be opened if we decide to continue the discussion on interim supply.
I do not know whether you must have a speech in your briefcase to have aspirations to be a leader of things, in the sense that Napoleon thought that every good soldier should have a field marshal's baton in his pack, but I believe that almost everyone in this house, without prodding, is capable of feeling that his nation, his constituency or the other members of his party require him to make a speech. In light of that I should just like to remind hon. members of some things of which they are, I am sure, well aware.
This session has been going on for a very long time. All records have been broken as to length of sessions and I am sure it will be many years before the situation is repeated. We have covered a tremendous number of topics and have put into effect a sizeable amount of legislation. In fact, Mr. Chairman, one of the ironies of the situation is this: If we are to be faced with an election campaign within a short period of time I suppose the theme of the government's campaign will be not unlike the theme contained in that Liberal pamphlet which most of us have been looking at recently, and I refer to the one with the beautiful printing, coloured 20220-823
Interim Supply
in red, yellow and grey with a maple leaf stylized to the extent that it almost is projected into the future, containing a long list of marvellous achievements of this government. The irony is that this government suggests that it is a poor, persecuted government, beset by a minority situation and a bunch of hatchet people in the opposition, particularly the right hon. leader of the official opposition. Yet it has attained a great deal. This is a contradiction.
In fairness and without being sarcastic in respect of what we have achieved, we have achieved this in spite of, or perhaps because of the fact that we have a minority parliament. I wonder whether some of these items would have been brought before us if we had not had a minority parliament. I wonder on the other hand whether it was necessary to have such a lengthy session. Here again, if you want to put the responsibility on anyone in particular it seems to me that the length of this session can be mainly explained in terms of what is an old H. L. Mencken expression, which I think I saw in a column by George Bain in which he stated that we had a federal government and Prime Minister of "doomocracy". It is because of that fact that we have had this long and extremely dragging session.
So many of the events of this session seem to be so far back in time that they have become almost ancient history. How many of us remember the Girouard affair, and that rollicking time we had at the sessions of the committee on privileges and elections. How many of us remember the hon. member for Renfrew South and the hon. member for Bow River giving us a sort of stylized debate, such as the one which took place between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas? That seems almost too far in the past to remember, yet it took place during this session. I wonder how many of us have forgotten about the Pearson film and how that great artistic masterpiece was denied to a large Canadian audience because of factors that are still not clear?
It is still on the order paper.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, as one hon. member has suggested, this is still on the order paper, but it has been forgotten and has been allowed to slip off into the past. However, that Pearson film incident occurred during this lengthy session.
We have been involved in many things during this session, but I think the time has

Interim Supply
come when we should pack it up as quickly as possible and get on to what we anticipate will be a good minority situation. Let us move on to the anticipated speech from the throne which will contain some other things which perhaps will fall flat, as did some of the measures that were heralded at the outset of this session.
I think the end of this session was very apparent today when we looked around this chamber and noted a large absentee situation. This is the time of the week when we can expect most members to be in the house because they all hold caucuses on Wednesday and because the "T-to-T" tradition does not affect attendance on Wednesday. During the question period today, when one would expect most members to be in attendance, there was a meagre representation. I do not think it is any reflection upon those members who were absent to mention this fact, because it is due probably to fatigue and the fact that the pension plan and opting out legislation are now out of the way.
Mr. Chairman, I think the silent members provide the best proof that this session should end as quickly as possible. Certainly that is the feeling of the members of this party. We believe that if we are not out of here by Friday we should all have our heads examined. The very least of our hopes is that all members in all parties feel the same way.
The final point I should like to make is that in this open end kind of situation, with interim supply before us it sometimes just takes one or two speeches on the same theme, a temper lost and the whole thing can blow up again resulting in the session marching on almost interminably. I mention this as a warning, or a suggestion if you wish, to those individuals who sit mainly in the treasury benches, in the hope that they will continue to practice as much restraint as they possibly can during the next short period of time in order to keep the spirit of this place amiable, so that we can tidy up the business of this session and get on to the new session. That is certainly the wish of this party. But in conclusion let me say that we do have those speeches in our briefcases or in our desks.

Mr. Chairman, I should like first of all to tell the house, on behalf of our party, that we have no intention to delay the passage of interim supply, because in the past, it used to be passed rather promptly. As a matter of fact,

it is only in the last two years that interim supply has given rise to extended debates.
I should like, however, to take this opportunity to raise three points which come to my mind in particular and are of concern to me and to a great number of Canadians in my area and throughout the country.
I should like first of all to call the attention of the house and of the ministers concerned, more particularly the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) and the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), to a brief submitted to the Minister of Agriculture last week and to which very little attention seems to have been given.
This brief from the Saguenay federation of the catholic farmers' union was prepared following a most unfortunate experience that farmers in the Saguenay area went through last year, first as a result of a hail storm which caused extensive damage in a certain sector and then because of bad weather during the year.
As a matter of fact, the Saguenay had rains which were more than persistent and, to all practical purposes, farmers were unable to sow. And what they did sow did not grow and, because of persistent bad weather, they were unable to get in what had managed to grow.
I should like to put on record the introductory letter to this brief. It is so explicit that it should be printed in Hansard. That letter was written in Chicoutimi last March 19 and is addressed to Hon. Harry Hays, Minister of Agriculture. I quote:
Honourable Minister:
As you learned from Hon. Alcide Courcy, Quebec's minister of agriculture, a very large number of farms in this province suffered considerably from the bad weather during all last year's farming season.
With regard to the Saguenay-Lake St. John region, the farmers lost approximately $5 million, which makes it a disaster farming area.
In case of serious disaster, the international practice is for the state to help the victims, even when they are insured. Many countries even provide assistance for citizens of other countries in times of disaster.
When the agricultural district of Saguenay-Lake St. John was struck by disaster, we asked the help of the Quebec government and we insisted that the province seek federal assistance.
Now, the Quebec minister of agriculture has forwarded to us a copy of your letter which is, for us, nearly the equivalent of a polite refusal on the grounds that Quebec had not yet set up a crop insurance scheme.
We recognize that Quebec farmers should enjoy the benefits of crop insurance since we have been advocating such coverage for years, but we must stress that only a few provinces have set up crop insurance programs until now and that this type

of legislation is more difficult of application in Quebec than in provinces where agriculture is a highly specialized industry.
Mr. Minister, we cannot accept to see the Canadian government hesitate this way to give assistance to the farmers of the Saguenay-Lake St. John area, in such distressing circumstances, when we know that they have already helped people of various classes, in Canada as well as abroad.
Is it necessary to remind you, Mr. Minister, that since 1962, for instance, Canada has given assistance to people from the following countries, for the following disasters:
Countries	Disasters
India-Ceylon	Tidal wave
South Viet Nam	Civil war
Cyprus	Civil war
West Pakistan	Cyclone
British Malaya	Civil war
British West Indies	Cyclone
The Caribbean Islands	Cyclone
Brazil	Famine
Barbados	Epidemic
Yugoslavia	Earthquake
Mr. Chairman, I do not see what assistance we can afford a country entangled in a civil war. I could go on citing instances where Canada helped other countries which had been plagued with calamities.
We should rejoice at the fact that Canada could assist those needy people, but we should also admit that we must impress upon the cabinet that a favourable decision be taken as soon as possible, in order that assistance be granted the farmers in the Saguenay-Lake St. John district who are seeking government help in this brief.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that this brief is most complete, since it analyses all the events which happened in 1964, together with the losses incurred by the farmers in the said district. It is well drafted and well presented, and I believe that after the ministers have taken cognizance of it, they should act immediately.
Mr. Chairman, I hope that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Beer) who is present here will bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture, so the government will take into consideration the possibility and the necessity of assisting the Saguenay-Lake St. John district. The brief also suggests that the government should assist those farmers to the extent of $12.11 per acre. In my opinion, this is not an arbitrary amount; that figure was established after lengthy studies, as will be seen. This brief is objective; it was prepared carefully, and the government should take action on it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Is the hon. member suggesting there has been some reluctance on the part of the federal government to assist and is he aware that when assistance is required in these distressed areas the initiative has to be taken by the province?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, of course I am aware of that, but if the hon. member had been here at the beginning when I was reading the letter he would have noticed that this was done. A brief was addressed to Hon. Mr. Courcy of Quebec and was forwarded to Ottawa by the minister of agriculture of Quebec. An answer was sent by the federal Minister of Agriculture to Hon. Alcide Courcy and in that letter the minister was apparently quite reluctant to assist in that case. I do not know why, because it seems to me that this is the first time we have had a really good case to present. We have always been told in the past to put our case clearly. I think this is the clearest case we can put before the government for the purpose of asking for some sort of assistance to agriculture in the Saguenay district.

Mr. Chairman, that was the point which I wanted to raise about agriculture, and I hope that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture will bring the matter to the attention of ministers concerned. At any rate, I intend to meet the ministers concerned, because I am convinced that they must do something. In the past various Canadian areas have been helped and I feel that farmers of the Saguenay area are as entitled as any other group to some federal assistance.
I admit that a request for assistance must be made by the provincial government. However, this request was made, and I hope that the federal government will act upon it.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with another matter and I am glad to see that the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) is in his seat. It is the famous matter of the designated areas. I wonder if it has become an obsession on my part, but in the last two years I think I have been the first to make representations to the minister for my town and my area to be recognized as designated areas so that they may take advantage of the benefits provided by the legislation. 1 admit that those benefits have not been necessarily useful to other areas, as, for instance, the Chicoutimi, Port Alfred and other surrounding regions, which were chosen as designated areas and where very few industries have come to settle.

Interim Supply
It seems that the benefits have not been quite good enough to attract industries.
On the other hand, the St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville area was selected as a designated area. Since it is almost in the outskirts of Montreal, this area was in a better position to attract industries which could profit by the economic advantages. In addition to the attraction of the Montreal area market there was also that of the tax abatements, which was most interesting for the industries going into that area, and more particularly into St. Jean, Valleyfield and Beauharnois.
On several occasions the minister stated that consideration was being given to the question of designated areas, that it was realized that the first criteria were not necessarily the best, but that it was probably the best that had come to mind at that time.
I agree with him that the task of establishing criteria taking into account all the objectives and all the problems is not the easiest thing to do, but I do want to say to the minister that he cannot split the Saguenay-Lake St. John area into separate sectors, because it is a state within a state, if you wish, or a province within a province, due to its remoteness from large centres. In fact, we have to go 150 miles through the woods before we reach any large centre.
The area is economically isolated, but highly developed. Its development has been fantastic in the last few years, but at this time it requires very special attention on the part of both provincial and federal authorities.
When the minister decides on the criteria to designate those new areas, I think that he will have to make allowance for the particular circumstances that exist in the Saguenay-Lake St. John area. The area is a closed economic unit and you cannot isolate a sector to help it without giving rise to some discrimination in the area.
I hope that the minister will designate the whole Saguenay-Lake St. John area, with very special points, so that the economic handicap due to our remoteness from large centres might be offset by tax benefits which will induce business firms to come and develop this beautiful area where I live and which I have the pleasure of representing.
Mr. Chairman, at the present time there are major business concerns in the Saguenay area: paper, aluminum; there is reasonably good agriculture, in the years when weather permits. But in my opinion, we must make an effort in order to avoid a repetition in the

Saguenay area of the experience which took place in the Gaspe peninsula.
Recently I met someone who works on the Gaspe peninsula development project and who told me that it was very difficult because in this area there has been an exodus of qualified personnel due to the fact that for too long that depressing situation was allowed to go on. The majority of those who, in their sphere and in their area, might have made a good contribution as economic qualified personnel, had to leave the Gaspe peninsula to go to Montreal, Quebec city, Ontario and even to the United States. We have witnessed, in the Gaspe peninsula, such a distressing situation that there were only young people, older people or children left there. There were very few people in their forties, having sufficient training to start economic undertakings. At the present time, that is one of the problems faced by a group of people from the province of Quebec who are attempting to give an economic impetus to the Gaspe peninsula. There is a lack of executives and also, to a certain extent, a lack of qualified people in various economic sectors, which makes the work still more difficult.
Mr. Chairman, such a situation may arise in the Saguenay area if we allow the present economic conditions to go on. In the Saguenay area, there are 250,000 people living in a territory about 100 miles long and 25 miles wide. There are large undertakings providing a more than abundant purchasing power in the area. But, at the present time, there is one thing which strikes the population and which concerns us. Let us take a typical example. In my town of Alma, the budget of the school board amounts to $3 million. There are technical schools, classical colleges; in short, we have a very good school system.
The problem at the present time is that as soon as our young people are educated, they must leave the area as they cannot be absorbed on the local market. In my opinion, this is a very bad thing as we thus lose our best people. We cannot afford to lose these young people to whose education we have contributed by our savings.
In my opinion, human capital is the primary resource of an area. It is this capital that must be developed and it is toward this end that our efforts are bent in the Saguenay area. But if we cannot give our human capital opportunities in our midst, it will have to leave and work to the advantage of other areas. We will have paid for nothing as far as the

economy of the area is concerned. In terms of the individual, there is no problem, because no matter where the citizen of Saguenay goes to make a living, if we gave him a sound education, he will bring along that good economic and social education to the community where he will live. But on the local economic level, it is a tragedy which we must put an end to, and I hope that the minister will pay very special and particular attention to the Saguenay region before it is too late.
There are some 600 to 700 engineers and technicians in the Saguenay region; there are executives in large industries; there are laboratories, such as Alcan, available to small enterprises. Alcan is prepared to assist them at all times with its own technicians. We only need a little assistance in fact, very little from the governments, in order to start the economy moving but at the present time, such assistance is not forthcoming.
I hope the minister will give very special attention to this matter, in order that the Saguenay area may know again the economic development it experienced in the past.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot help but support the remarks just made by the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard), which riding is next to that of Lapointe.
The Saguenay area-the realm of Saguenay, as it is often called-is, of course, one of the most beautiful in Canada. Unfortunately, it is tremendously in need of help, from the industrial point of view, at the present time. I trust the Minister of Industry and Defence Production (Mr. Drury) will co-operate in that area to promote the establishment and the development of new industries.
As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickers-gill) is also in his seat, besides the Minister of Industry and Defence Production, it seems to me this is the time to speak about the Canadian National Railways, which are at present endeavouring to set up an industrial unit in the municipality of Jonquiere.
It seems to me that if two ministers as qualified as the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Industry and Defence Production join forces so that this initiative of the Canadian National Railways materializes, we can expect great achievements that could contribute to the economic development of the whole area.
Today, Mr. Chairman, I should like to talk on another question which is, I think, rather important.
I have already had the opportunity, since coming to this house, to talk of bilingualism
Interim Supply
in the C.N.R. I think that since that time there has been an improvement. I believe that the
president of this railway company is making efforts to improve the situation. I often receive many comments to the effect that this situation has improved. Of course, a radical change cannot be made overnight, but I feel that the changes have been satisfactory, and we hope that this will continue. But all those changes, we have got them because we claimed them forcefully.
The same thing happened for Air Canada. We have requested many, many times, through questions asked in this house, that Air Canada favour more bilingualism.
Moreover, it is those two large corporations, the C.N.R. and Air Canada, which invite our fellow citizens to visit the country from coast to coast. Therefore, it is desirable that Canadian citizens feel at home everywhere in this country and when they make trips by plane or train, that they may be understood in their own language.
Today I should like to insist especially on bilingualism in the R.C.M.P. But before coming to that matter, I want to say that Air Canada brought many improvements as did the C.N.R. and I think that it is in order to congratulate Air Canada for the improvements made in the field of bilingualism. There is still much to do, but nevertheless there have been improvements, following repeated requests on our part. And so, today, I would like to make the same request in respect of the R.C.M.P.
The R.C.M.P. comes under the Department of Justice. For many decades, we have had several French Canadians as ministers of justice. First, there was Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe; then, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent and, after him Hon. Lionel Chevrier. We have now the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Favreau), another French Canadian.
In between those four French Canadian ministers, two English speaking ministers perfectly bilingual, held that portfolio, Hon. Mr. Fulton and Hon. Mr. Fleming.
And yet, even if there were four French-Canadian ministers and two bilingual ministers in the last decades heading the Department of Justice, the R.C.M.P. remains one of the departments where it is difficult at the present time to have bilingualism. In fact, that body cannot understand the efforts being made elsewhere and does not try in the least to establish bilingualism as it should be understood in Canada at the present time.

Interim Supply
It was found recently during the Dorion inquiry that even the R.C.M.P.'s manual was not yet bilingual. Here, in the house, parliamentary rules and forms were not bilingual but, less than a year ago we obtained a translation.
However, as far as the R.C.M.P. is concerned, questions had to be asked; in short, the situation had to be exposed before the courts in order that the people could at last realize that the R.C.M.P.'s manual used by the members of that police force was not even written or translated in French. This is pushing unilingualism a little too far.
Most lawyers acting for the R.C.M.P. are nearly always-even if the investigation in question is held in Montreal or Ottawa, as in the case of the Dorion inquiry-Toronto lawyers who do not understand one word of French, when all the witnesses and the lawyers of the other parties are French Canadians. As a matter of fact, in the case of that investigation there was only one individual who did not understand French and that was the R.C.M.P.'s lawyer.
I think that has been noted, because in the committee on privileges and elections when the question of the operation of the R.C.M.P. came up it was asked, probably for the first time, that a French Canadian lawyer represent the R.C.M.P. and try, in co-operation with that police force, to establish that summons and warrants should be drawn up in both languages and not only in English.
About this inquiry, I would like to refer to a fact deriving from a statement made in the house by Hon. Lionel Chevrier, the then minister of justice, on June 25, 1963. He said, in reply to a question I put to him, and which may be found at page 1536 of Hansard of June 25, 1963, in the right hand column:
But, for the information of the hon. member, I should like to say that when a violation occurs on parliament hill or on drives or roads falling under the jurisdiction of the R.C.M.P., it is the practice to issue warrants in both languages.
This is what was stated by Hon. Lionel Chevrier, the then minister of justice.
In order to check whether this was being done, I had the opportunity to put the question to members of the R.C.M.P. who were giving evidence under oath, before the committee on privileges and elections, and I put the question after having repeated this statement from Hon. Lionel Chevrier, which I quote again:
But, for the information of the hon. member, I should like to say that when a violation occurs on parliament hill or on drives or roads falling under the jurisdiction of the R.C.M.P., it is the practice to issue warrants in both languages.

I was putting the question to Constable Stamler, in charge of the warrants and summons office. I said:
Has that statement of Hon. Lionel Chevrier ever been passed on to you by some of your superiors?
Here is what he answered:

No, of course not.

In a statement made in the House of Commons in June 1963, the then minister of justice said that it was the practice of the R.C.M.P. to issue summons and warrants in both languages.
So one could expect the R.C.M.P. to be aware of that statement. But when I asked Constable Stamler:
Has that statement by Hon. Mr. Chevrier ever been passed on to you by some of your superiors?
The answer was-and this took place on March 2, 1965:

No, of course not.

And I went on to ask:
Have your superiors ever talked to you about it?
The answer was:

No.

At this stage, I must point out that I have the bilingual report at hand and that when a question is asked in French, I have the French text, whereas when the reply is given in English, I look up the English text.
When I asked Constable Stamler:
Then, it was not a rule in the R.C.M.P.?
His answer was:

The national capital commission falls into four different courts; one of the courts is the Hull court, and if the violation occurs on the Quebec side we do serve these summonses and execute the warrant in the French language.

And again, I asked:
In French only or in the two languages?
Constable Stamler answered:

In the French language if the person charged has a French name.

Thus, they use a warrant in French, but only in the province of Quebec and only if the person has a French name. Please note the other answers of that constable; continuing my questioning I asked him:
In French only or in both languages?
If the person in Hull has an English name, you serve it in English?
Constable Stamler's answer was this:

If he was charged in the province of Quebec, yes, it would be in English only.

Then, Mr. Chairman, when it became somewhat embarrassing, the chairman declared that it was out of order, that it was irrelevant to the matter in hand. Yet, the questions I had asked as to the practices of the R.C.M.P. were rather simple, namely: In what language are the warrants you serve in Ontario, and in the rest of Canada? The answer was: In English only. But whenever they have to deal with an English Canadian or a person bearing an English name in the province of Quebec, the warrant is served in English. It is in French only when the person concerned lives in the province of Quebec and bears a French name.
Then, it is in English, even in the province of Quebec, if the person bears an English name. Would you call that bilingualism? I would say it is a one-way bilingualism, with English everywhere. But, as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, it seems to me it has the same rights as the other provinces especially as regards the R.C.M.P.
Mind you, the question was asked with respect to a statement made by the minister of justice of the day, Hon. Lionel Chevrier, who said that when it dealt with an offence committed on parliament hill or a federal driveway, the warrant should be issued in both languages. Now, this took place at the airport on federal government property, and the warrant could have been served to me in both languages.
That is why the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) asked Constable Stamler, in English, the following question:

Are you aware of any regulation or law or procedure which demands that the summons or warrant, which is at issue here, be in the French language in the province of Ontario?
A. No. It is my understanding it has to be in the English language only.

Then, what was the meaning of the statement made by Hon. Lionel Chevrier? What was the meaning of the statements of the then minister of justice who was responsible for the R.C.M.P.? Statements are made in the house just to show off in front of the people in the galleries, and back at the office they give opposite instructions. We should know what happens in the Department of Justice, whether they tell one thing to members in the house and the contrary to members of the R.C.M.P.

Allow me to quote, for instance, a sentence of the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien):
