speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
First, with regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Wellington South, namely that the government entered into this arrangement with the United States under the power granted to it to modify tariffs rather than through the legislative process. This is what has been done, but at the same time it has been stated in the house both by the Prime Minister and by myself that the government would welcome the opportunity for a full debate on this particular topic as soon as the timetable allows.
I myself look forward with anticipation to such a debate because in my view this agreement does hold out very substantial advantages for the manufacturing industry in Canada. I will be glad of the opportunity to set out at some length the advantages and the benefits which are expected to flow from it. Unfortunately, as the house knows, we have been preoccupied for a long period of time with a number of high priority items and we have not been able to do all we would have wished. This is one of the things I would like to see done and I hope an opportunity will present itself fairly early in the new session.
As far as Canadian content is concerned, I think there is some misconception about the significance of the previous references to percentage of Canadian content and the current references to dollar values in the absolute. Let me put it another way. In the arrangements which antedated the provision for stripped engine transmission plants, motor manufacturers in Canada could import into this country free of duty a number of items specified in the tariff, provided they achieved a commonwealth content, a certain percentage depending on their volume of production. This means that the total expenditure in the commonwealth in respect of a given car had to be a percentage of the total cost of the car, and if a manufacturer were able to achieve this-in large operations a 60 per cent figure-he would then have the right to import certain items listed in the tariff duty free.
Under the present plan, which contemplates duty free entry of original equipment and cars into the United States from Canada, Canadian motor car manufacturers-all of them, not merely the three mentioned by the hon. member for Wellington South-will have to do a number of things, the result of which

will be in the aggregate an increase in the production in Canada and an increase in over-all automotive activity here. Within the next three years this will mean an increase of about one third, or 30 per cent over the 1964 level.
This will be achieved by having the motorcar manufacturers undertake, in respect of cars that they will produce in Canada for the domestic market to continue to incorporate in those cars Canadian added value in an amount not less than that for the base year, or in other words a floor. In addition to that, they will have to undertake to incorporate in all cars manufactured for the Canadian market Canadian added value to the extent of 60 per cent of the value of the increased sales to the Canadian market. In addition to that, they will undertake individually to achieve a specified figure, which is different for each firm, in respect of additional Canadian production. This has reference to the three levels, one superimposed on another. It is as a result of this that manufacturers in Canada will increase by one third the value of automotive manufacturing in Canada in the next three years.
We are persuaded, as I think all automotive industry people are, that this plan will result in a substantial increase in activity in the whole automotive field. There are undoubtedly going to be some changes both in technique of production and, in some instances, the location of production. The gross result will be a substantial increase.
My department is very concerned to see that where changes take place they take place in as orderly a fashion as possible, and we are paying special attention to those who are fearful of severe dislocation. We are also taking steps to see that what assistance the federal government is able to give is given in order to make the transition easier for all.

I should like to take this opportunity to thank the minister for what certainly sounded like a very clear and precise explanation of some of the problems that have been worrying a great many of us in this house. Naturally I will want to examine his remarks very carefully, because of their technical nature. However, I understood him to state that in respect of the increase in the number of cars produced by manufacturers for sale in Canada, that the Canadian content would remain at the fixed 60 per cent figure.

In this same period domestic production will go from the $60 million floor which was mentioned, based on 60 per cent content, to $72 million if we take 60 per cent of $20 million which is $12 million and add that to the $60 million. There will also be an additional figure, and here I get into difficulties. However, without disclosing precisely what the figure is it will be of the order of $250 million. It is quite clear that under the plan domestic production is going to rise more rapidly than the increase in domestic sales. It can be converted into content, of course, but one wants to get away from the word "content". The essential fact is that domestic production is going to increase more rapidly than domestic sales.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise a matter that is of considerable concern to practically every gold mining community in Canada. The concern is brought about by not one but two policies of the present government, their policy toward the gold mining industry as a whole and their policy with regard to the Canadian exchange fund.
We are all aware that for the past 30 years the price of gold has been tied to a figure of $35 per ounce in United States dollars, but possibly we are not all aware that during the last 25 years the number of operating

gold mines in Canada has dropped from 254 to 42 at present and that the number of miners employed in the industry has dropped since 1941 from 32,551 to 13,798 as of late 1964. I should like members of the committee to realize for a moment just what this means. In the first place, it means that there are 212 mines which are no longer buying timber, steel, machinery, hoists, cable, blasting powder, fuses and the thousands of other things that a gold mine uses. They are no longer paying taxes or wages. It means that some 18,753 jobs have been lost in this industry. At an average of $5,000 a year, this amounts to almost $100 million. In that regard one must realize that each one of these jobs means a breadwinner and householder. It means that families have been uprooted all across the country. It means that millions of dollars have been paid out of the unemployment insurance fund to people who have lost their jobs in this industry. Furthermore, it means that many thousands of jobs have been lost indirectly in the manufacturing industry, the consumer goods industry and in the stores and service establishments that serve these communities.
There is something else I think we should realize. These jobs have been lost in the very field that is of the greatest concern to this country today because these are unskilled and semi-skilled jobs in a field where automation is becoming an increasing problem. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, this situation has meant that the development of the north country has been held back because of this policy, and certainly we have had an example of this in Timmins in the last year. When Texas Gulf made their big strike last year it stimulated the search for minerals. As a result not only were jobs provided in the search itself but since that time two more properties have been found and a third one is to be announced shortly, I am told. All this has happened just because a new mine opened which stimulated the search for minerals, and this will have a great effect on the eoonomy of the country as a whole.
I think we should all realize that the only way the gold mining industry can be revived is by an increase in the price of gold. But the only policy that this government and the previous government have applied to the problem has been that set forth in the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. This policy has been in effect for some 17 of the last 24 years to which I have referred. It has not reversed the trend. In fact, I would say it has only slowed it down very slightly and

if it is carried on in its present form I would say on the basis of the figures I have given it can only be classed as a sort of futile old age pension to a dying industry.
In my view the government, as I hope to point out, has been assisting in the death of the industry by strangulation, and I would say this is just as disastrous to the economy of the country as floods, forest fires or drought. The process is slow and insidious and is not as dramatic, with the result that the situation does not receive the same attention. Furthermore, I would say that the onus is on the government because not only the gold mining industry but the whole economy will be affected. I am not suggesting for one moment that the government can raise the price of gold unilaterally; that would be a ridiculous assumption. But there are ways in which the government can help and it is not making use of them at the present time.
This brings me to the second point I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, the policy of the government toward the Canadian exchange fund. As of November, 1964 Canada kept only 35 per cent of its exchange fund in gold, some $1,007 million, and 65 per cent in American dollars or some $1,736 million. I should like to compare this situation with that of some of the other western countries. For example, Germany keeps 63 per cent of its exchange fund in gold, Belgium 78 per cent, France 82 per cent, Great Britain 83 per cent, the Netherlands 84 per cent, Switzerland 89 per cent and the United States of America 99 per cent.
Two questions come to mind. Why does the United States keep 99 per cent of its exchange fund in gold and at the same time ask Canada to keep only 35 per cent of its exchange fund in gold? The second question is even more important. Why does Canada agree? This question was asked last December of the governor of the Bank of Canada and his reply raised two interesting points. First of all, it proved beyond any shadow of doubt that the responsibility rests solely with the Minister of Finance. I should like to quote from this letter from the governor to prove this. He said:
I should perhaps begin by pointing out that the exchange fund account is the property of the government of Canada and not the Bank of Canada, and it is the Minister of Finance who decides in what form the assets of the account should be held.
Then he goes on to give the reason they are doing this. I would say, Mr. Chairman, it is a rather lame reason. I quote:

Mr. Chairman, Canada is entering a period in which, more than ever before, the decisions concerning the country as a whole must be taken both by the federal and provincial governments. To achieve this goal, we have to take a new look at the whole Canadian system and the way it is operating now. Economic conditions, in the present context, are surely different from what they were a century ago.
Within the next few years we shall have to come up with bold solutions. We shall have to show some imagination when applying

Prior to the war of 1939-45, the sharing was proportionate to revenues among the three levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal.
During the last war the federal government took over the fields of taxation, thereby destroying provincial autonomy. Moreover, the federal government widened its range in the area of direct and indirect taxes, while not forgetting to increase the rates, apparently in order to fulfil its obligations.
~ After the war the needs of the provinces really came to the fore, because after being deprived of their properties, they found themselves in a deplorable financial situation. In the last few years, with the help of federal-provincial conferences, attempts have been made to reach a compromise. Since the federal government is unwilling to hand over to the provinces the fields of taxation it monopolized during the war, federal-provincial conferences always seem doomed to failure.
That is why today more than ever, since the provinces have priority needs, they insist on being treated fairly by the central government.
As a member from the province of Quebec I say that Quebec has priority needs.
Quebec needs its sources of income in order to develop its natural resources at a quick pace and to enable private enterprise to increase its production.
In public services there are municipalities, school boards, education, public health, social welfare and roads departments.
They say that in Quebec education will cost about $1 billion in 1967 in the field of health; investments will reach more than $30 million before 1967.
Mr. Chairman, so that a province can develop, meet its responsibilities, play its part, the central government must give back to the provinces their taxation rights.
After the second world war the Canadian economy had to adjust to new conditions. An economic recession had to be avoided. Our economy also had to be given new direction in order to ensure stability and minimize inflation. The provinces understood that situation. In short, the federal government had to give our post-war economy the means of providing Canadians with a standard of living to which they were entitled.
It was agreed that fiscal agreements with the provinces were to be temporary. The war is over and a state of emergency no

It has been recognized since confederation that the provinces wanted their jurisdiction to be respected. Quebec, among others, never missed a chance to let the federal government know about that. Today more than ever, the provinces maintain the same attitude.
Mr. Chairman, the province of Quebec is not a province like the others. The vast majority of the inhabitants of the province of Quebec are French Canadians. Within the whole of Canada, they are nevertheless a minority, an important minority established in this country for centuries, and this gives it particular rights and duties.
We demand that its traditions and characteristics be protected and maintained because they are a fundamental right. Quebec is the guardian of the French language and culture. That is why we often say that it is the mother country of all French speaking people in America. I will go even further and state that the city of Quebec which I have the honour to represent here is the cradle of French civilization in North America.
Canada, of which Quebec is a province, has a federal government which guarantees, through the British North America Act, the rights of French Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, for the past two or three years principles which were held to be sacred in the past are open to discussion not only in Quebec but throughout Canada and our party is not alien to the present turmoil.
Most politicians cannot wait to discuss the repatriation of the constitution.
For a strong Quebec the amendment to the constitution will have to include four points:
First, control over credit.
Second, control over imports and exports.
Third, control over immigration.
Fourth, return of taxation powers. Control over credit by the establishment of the bank of Quebec. The role of that bank will be:
1. To lend "new credit without interest" by means of scrip and paper currency:
(a) to the various government departments to finance public capital;

(b) to private financial institutions, if necessary, to finance private capital of individuals and firms.
2.	To require, in a scientific way, reimbursement of loans made to the various government departments or to private institutions according to the physical depreciation rate of production financed by the loan.
3.	To distribute to consumers, unconditionally their free share of social revenue by means of bonuses, family allowances, school and university allowances, pensions, dividends and compensated discount, under the immediate authority of the national credit commission.
The control of foreign trade is the second point we feel should be considered when amending the constitution. And to explain the reasons why we ask that Quebec be given control over its exports and imports, it is important first of all to agree on some principles.
First, the object of the economic order is to satisfy the consumers, nothing else.
Second, the object of industrial activities is to supply consumers with goods and services, and not work or jobs.
Third, the object of trade exchanges between two countries or of international trade is to supply the importing country with goods it cannot produce or cannot produce easily. In return, the importing country wants to export its excess goods to those who need them.
However, at the present time we are forced to the conclusion that the direct exchange of available surpluses is no longer a rule of international trade. Today export trade is carried on mainly for the purpose of keeping our plants and factories producing, and thereby sustaining employment. Lord Kynes very aptly described the situation when he said that the purpose of international trade is to export unemployment.
And that is why our views in the matter are definitely in line with Social Credit principles. In developed countries, such as ours, the control of production is such that enough production is possible to ensure to everyone a comfortable living. The production is there. It is merely a matter of distributing it properly.
The third point we deal with is the control of our immigration. As the federal government seems to realize more and more the unfairness of its immigration policy and seems to be willing to improve things in this department which allows criminals to take refuge in Canada, and as Quebec, under the pressure of the opposition, just made a timid first step in that field, it is important to point out that our policy is not irrelevant to this renewal.
